hits.name: GREG ISENBERG
hits.text:
A guy let Claude read his 1994 Jeep's engine computer through a $3 chip.

It found why the car kept failing smog, and he says it passed. 

The whole thing cost about $15 in parts, and it's free on GitHub. https://t.co/E9kOFaX8sq
hits.hook: A guy let Claude read his 1994 Jeep's engine computer through a $3 chip.  It found why the car kept failing smog, and he
hits.draft_en:
Greg Isenberg shared a project where someone let Claude read a 1994 Jeep's engine computer through a $3 chip. It found why the car kept failing smog and, by the owner's account, it then passed. About $15 in parts, free on GitHub (166k views, 1.7k bookmarks).

Agents get useful when you give them a real data port. What device do you own that already logs its own errors?
hits.video_tip: 8s: cheap chip plugged under a dashboard, laptop shows the fault code, agent explains it in one line.

hits.name: Alex Finn
hits.text:
You're not being ambitious enough with your AI

Run the reverse prompt below

The AI takes ALL the facts it knows about you, and finds the most ambitious project you can currently focus on

Prompt:

"Based on what you know about me, what's the most ambitious question/prompt I could send you? One that could lead to a breakthrough or idea that can change my life? Nothing is too ambitious (as long as it's possible)"

This is super powerful because the AI knows EVERYTHING about you. It's able to take the entire context of your life and uncover unknown unknowns you haven't thought of yet

It leans on the AI's super intelligence to come up with ambitious ideas, rather than your own limited current knowledge

Run this and let me know what you get (thanks to Dmitry for inspiring me to come up with this)
hits.hook: You're not being ambitious enough with your AI  Run the reverse prompt below  The AI takes ALL the facts it knows about
hits.draft_en:
Alex Finn's 'reverse prompt': ask your AI, based on what it knows about you, for the most ambitious question you could ask it (97k views, 2.4k bookmarks).

Useful as a brainstorm. Then do the boring part: pick one idea and write down how you'd check it's real before spending a week on it.
hits.video_tip: 7s: chat box, prompt typed, a long list appears, one item circled and a checklist underneath.

hits.name: GREG ISENBERG
hits.text:
New trend I'm observing:

1. Startup raises venture capital
2. Uses venture dollars to become creator 
3. Startup fails
4. Fall back on becoming a full-time creator and makes $500k-$5M/year as creator
5. Incubates other products bootstrapped
6. Never raises VC again
hits.hook: New trend I'm observing:  1. Startup raises venture capital 2. Uses venture dollars to become creator  3. Startup fails
hits.draft_en:
Greg Isenberg's new pattern: startup raises VC, uses it to build an audience, startup fails, founder becomes a full-time creator and incubates bootstrapped products, never raises again (10k views).

The audience outlived the company. If you're building, document it in public from day one.
hits.video_tip: 8s: a timeline of 6 steps, step 3 crossed out, step 4 glowing.

virals.angle: Give your agent a real port
virals.draft_en:
Someone let Claude read a 1994 Jeep's engine computer through a $3 chip. It found why the car kept failing smog. About $15 in parts, free on GitHub (via Greg Isenberg, 166k views).

The trick isn't the model. It's the cable. Find one thing you own that already logs errors and let an agent read it.
virals.video_tip: 8s: hand plugs a tiny board under the dash, laptop prints the fault, 'passed smog' stamp.

virals.angle: Ambitious prompt, then a reality check
virals.draft_en:
Alex Finn's reverse prompt is everywhere today: ask your AI for the most ambitious question you could ask it (97k views, 2.4k bookmarks). Ethan Mollick adds the catch: you still need some expertise to tell exciting results from wrong ones.

So run it, pick one idea, then list 3 checks you'd use to prove it's real.
virals.inspired_by: @AlexFinn reverse prompt (97k, 2.4k bookmarks) + @emollick ambition (55k) and expertise needed (11k)
virals.video_tip: 8s: wild idea on screen, then 3 checkboxes tick one by one.

virals.draft_en:
Pieter Levels pointed out X's rules: AI reply bots aren't permitted, and auto-pasting the same reply counts too. Simon Willison on the email version: 'Your post on [summary] caught my eye' (62k views).

Use AI to research the person. Write the one sentence yourself.
virals.inspired_by: @levelsio X rules on AI replies (18k) + @simonw templated emails (62k)
virals.video_tip: 7s: inbox of identical openers blurring, one short real note in focus.

virals.draft_en:
Danny Postma: Tobi's prompt 'scan this codebase for any implicit state machines and make it explicit' is insanely good on an old game codebase (47k views, 845 bookmarks).

Works beyond games: checkout flows, onboarding, anything with hidden 'modes'. Run it on your oldest file this weekend.
